1. PROJECT DETAILS
1.1. Summary Description of the Project
Lamantin mangrove restoration and conservation project, developed by Blue Coast Carbon, is a community-
based large-scale mangrove conservation project in Guinea, West Africa.
The project will be located in an area along the northern coasts of Guinea, covering a total of 73,751
hectares of mangrove forests.
Mangroves are coastal forests that grow where ocean water, freshwater, and land meet. They are amongst
the planet’s most productive and complex ecosystems, and are recognized for their superior carbon
sequestration capabilities compared to terrestrial forests. Throughout West Africa, the livelihoods of coastal
populations depend heavily on access to natural resources. Mangroves are integral to many of those
resources, providing wood and non-wood forest products, coastal protection, conservation of biological
diversity, provision of habitat, spawning grounds and nutrients for a variety of fish and shellfish, and salt
production. West Africa’s coastlines have some of the highest and most rapidly growing populations. Many
communities rely on mangrove wood as a primary fuel source for curing fish and other purposes, and urban
expansion and intensifying demands for charcoal, fuel wood, and land for agriculture are growing drivers
of mangrove deforestation and degradation1. These factors, combined with rising sea levels, erosion from
extreme weather, and more intense storm surges, represent significant and growing threats to mangroves2.
The overall project objective is to generate high-quality carbon credits based on greenhouse gases (GHGs)
emission reduction and avoidance, that will sustainably finance the project and result in economic benefits
for the local communities. GHGs emission reductions are expected to be generated by avoiding unplanned
deforestation by providing alternative income to local communities through the implementation of a series
of activities, including those supporting the use of efficient cookstoves, solar salt production systems,
education campaigns, and supporting the development of apiculture, aquaculture and ecotourism.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) removals will be generated by restoring areas of degraded mangrove forests with the
involvement of local communities, supporting local livelihoods and alleviating poverty. An ecosystem-based
approach will be used for habitat restoration, aiming at improving hydrology and environmental conditions,
with minimal need for re-planting.
The project will restore a total of 2,725 hectares of degraded mangrove forests and protect a total of
73,751 hectares from deforestation, contributing to the protection of coastal communities from climate
change, the conservation of the world’s biodiversity and to mitigating climate change.
1 USAID, 2014, Workshop Report: West Africa Regional Mangroves and Climate Change, U.S. Agency for
International Development
2 Corcoran, E., Ravilious, C., and Skuja, M., 2007, Mangroves of western and central Africa: UNEP/Earthprint 26

Page 6
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
6
The project’s climate benefits over the crediting period include the sequestration and avoided emission of
3,374,658 tCO2e.

The project does not have an audit history yet. The first audit will be completed at the time of project
validation and initial verification.
1.3. Sectoral Scope and Project Type
Sectoral scope 14 Agriculture, forestry, and other land use (AFOLU)
AFOLU project category3 Wetlands Restoration and Conservation (WRC)
Project activity type Restoring wetland ecosystem (RWE) combined with ARR
Conservation of intact wetlands (CIW) – Avoiding Unplanned
Wetland Degradation – combined with REDD+
1.4. Project Eligibility
1.4.1. General eligibility
The project is eligible under the scope of the VCS Program, as it aims at enhancing the sequestration and
avoiding the emission of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) by mangrove forest
conservation and ecosystem restoration.
Project activities are supported by the VCS methodologies VM0033 and VM0007. Furthermore, the project
does not involve any of the activity listed in Table 1 of the VCS Standard v4.7.
The project will initiate the pipeline listing process within three years of the project start date and complete
validation within eight years of the project start date.
The applied methodologies VM0033 and VM0007 are applicable to WRC and REDD+ projects under the
VCS Program.

1.4.2. AFOLU project eligibility
The project falls under the AFOLU project categories WRC, ARR, and REDD+ as defined in Appendix 1
Eligible AFOLU project categories of the VCS Standard v4.7. Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3 present the VCS
Standard’s requirements and how the project will comply with them.
Table 1 Compliance with eligibility conditions of WRC projects (from Appendix 1 of the VCS Standard V4.7).
Eligibility condition Compliance
Eligible WRC activities are those that increase net
GHG removals by restoring wetland ecosystems or
that reduce GHG emissions by rewetting or
avoiding the degradation of wetlands.
The project activities will increase net GHG
removals by restoring degraded mangrove forests
and will reduce GHG emissions by avoiding
additional degradation and deforestation.
The project area shall meet an internationally
accepted definition of wetland, such as from the
IPCC, Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, those
established by law or national policy, or those with
broad agreement in the peer-reviewed scientific
literature for specific countries or types of
wetlands.
‘Wetlands include any land that is covered or
saturated by water for all or part of the year, and
that does not fall into the Forest Land, Cropland, or
Grassland categories’(IPCC)4.
The project involves areas of mangrove forests in
coastal wetlands, i.e. daily affected by
astronomical tides and saline water.
Common wetland types include peatland, salt
marsh, tidal freshwater marsh, mangroves, wet
floodplain forests, prairie potholes and seagrass
meadows.
The project area is mainly covered by mangrove
forests.
Activities that generate net reductions of GHG
emissions from wetlands are eligible as WRC
projects or combined category projects (such as
REDD on peatland).
The project will increase net GHG removals by
restoring the mangrove ecosystem, combined with
conservation of existing mangrove forests.
4 Chapter 7 Wetlands, Volume 4, 2006 IPCC Guidelines

Page 8
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
8
Activities that actively lower the water table depth
in wetlands are not eligible.
Project activities will not lower the water table
depth.
Eligible WRC activities include Restoring Wetland
Ecosystems (RWE): This category includes
activities that reduce GHG emissions or increase
carbon sequestration in a degraded wetland
through restoration conditions, sediment supply,
salinity characteristics, water quality and/or native
plant communities. For the purpose of these
requirements, restoration activities are those that
result in the reestablishment of ecological
processes, functions, and biotic and/or abiotic
linkages that lead to persistent, resilient systems
integrated within the landscape.
The project will restore degraded wetlands by
means of activities aimed at restoring natural
conditions to allow for spontaneous habitat
recovery, such as removal of pollution and
restoration of natural hydrological conditions to
allow for optimum mangrove growth.
The abiotic conditions will be carefully assessed
before the start of the activities to identify the most
suitable interventions.
Conservation of Intact Wetlands (CIW): This
category includes activities that reduce GHG
emissions by avoiding degradation and/or the
conversion of wetlands that are intact or partially
altered while still maintaining their natural
functions, including hydrological conditions,
sediment supply, salinity characteristics, water
quality and/or native plant communities.
The project involves activities aimed at protecting
intact wetlands thus reducing GHGs emissions by
avoiding degradation of mangrove forests. These
include the promotion of sustainable systems for
salt production and efficient cook stoves, together
with education and awareness programmes.
Avoiding Planned Wetland Degradation (APWD):
This activity reduces GHG emissions by avoiding
degradation of wetlands, or further degradation in
partially drained wetlands that are legally
authorized and documented for conversion.
Avoiding Unplanned Wetland Degradation (AUWD):
This activity reduces GHG emissions by avoiding
unplanned degradation of wetlands, or by avoiding
further degradation in partially degraded wetlands.
The activities of this project fall under the scope of
Avoiding Unplanned Deforestation and/or
Degradation, as there are no set plans for any
activity that would cause wetland degradation.
Activities where drainage is continued or
maintained are not eligible. This includes, for
example, projects that require the maintenance of
drainage channels to maintain the pre-project
drainage level on a partially drained peatland (e.g.,
Drainage will not be performed.

Page 9
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
9
where periodic deepening may be needed to
counteract peat subsidence).
Projects that allow selective harvesting that results
in a lowering of the water table depth (e.g., by
extracting timber using drainage canals) or affects
the ability of vegetation to act as a major
hydrological regulation device (e.g., extracting
trees which support the peat body) are not eligible.
This project will not allow selective harvesting.
Activities that generate net GHG emission
reductions by combining other AFOLU project
activities with wetlands restoration or conservation
activities are eligible as WRC combined projects.
RWE may be implemented without further
conversion of land use, or it may be combined with
ARR, ALM, IFM, REDD or ACoGS activities, referred
to as ARR+RWE, ALM+RWE, IFM+RWE,
REDD+RWE or ACoGS+RWE, respectively. CIW may
be implemented on non-forest land or combined
with IFM, REDD or ACoGS activities, referred to as
IFM+CIW, REDD+CIW or ACoGS+CIW, respectively.
The baseline scenario in this project is degraded
wetland and forest with deforestation and
degradation as the main land use. Project activities
include restoration of wetlands (mangroves) and
revegetation. There is no further conversion of land
use. Therefore, this project is a WRC project
combining ARR and RWE.
Combined category projects shall use the relevant
WRC requirements and the respective AFOLU
project category requirements for quantifying GHG
emissions/removals unless the former may be
deemed de minimis or conservatively excluded.

Table 3 Compliance with eligibility conditions of REDD+ projects (from Appendix 1 of the VCS Standard V4.7).
Eligibility condition Compliance
The project area shall meet an internationally
accepted definition of forest, such as those based
on UNFCCC host-country thresholds or FAO
definitions and shall qualify as forest for a
minimum of 10 years before the project start date.
The definition of forest may include mature forests,
secondary forests, and degraded forests. Under
the VCS Program, secondary forests are
considered to be forests that have been cleared
and have recovered naturally and that are at least
10 years old and meet the lower bound of the
forest threshold parameters at the start of the
project.
According to the UNFCCC, a forest is defined as an
area of land spanning more than 0.05-1.0 hectares
with tree crown cover (or equivalent stocking level)
of more than 10-30% with trees having the
potential to reach a minimum height of 2-5 meters
at maturity in situ.
The mangrove forests in the project area have met
such requirements over the last 10 years.
Activities covered under the REDD project category
are those that are designed to stop planned
(designated and sanctioned) deforestation or
unplanned (unsanctioned) deforestation and/or
degradation. Avoided planned degradation is
classified as IFM.
Activities for this project are designed to stop
unplanned deforestation and/or degradation.
Activities that stop unsanctioned deforestation
and/or illegal degradation (such as removal of
fuelwood or timber extracted by non-
concessionaires) on lands that are legally
sanctioned for timber production are eligible as
REDD activities. However, activities that reduce or
stop logging only, followed by protection, on forest
lands legally designated or sanctioned for forestry
The activities do not stop logging and are not on
the IFM scope. They stop unsanctioned
deforestation and unplanned degradation.

activities are included within IFM. Projects that
include both avoided unplanned deforestation
and/or degradation as well as stopping sanctioned
logging activities, shall follow the REDD guidelines
for the unplanned deforestation and/or
degradation and the IFM guidelines for the
sanctioned logging activities, and shall follow the
requirements set out in Section 3.6.2.
Eligible REDD activities include:
1) Avoiding Planned Deforestation (APD): This
category includes activities that reduce net GHG
emissions by permanently stopping or reducing
deforestation on forest lands that are legally
authorized and documented for conversion.
Planned deforestation encompasses activities
where a forest system would have been cleared
and replaced by a different forest system with a
lower carbon stock and where the recovery of
timber was not the primary objective of the initial
forest clearance.
2) Avoiding Unplanned Deforestation and/or
Degradation (AUDD): This category includes
activities that reduce net GHG emissions by
stopping deforestation and/or degradation of
degraded to mature forests that would have
occurred in any forest configuration.
The activities of this project fall under the scope of
Avoiding Unplanned Deforestation and/or
Degradation

1.8. Ownership
To manage the project and legally secure ownership over the carbon credits generated by the project, Blue
Coast Carbon is seeking a concession agreement with the government. The Ministry of Environment and
Sustainable Development (MEDD) issued Blue Coast Carbon a letter on the 16th December 2025 approving
the development and finalisation of this project. The letter gives Blue Coast Carbon the right to list the
project as under development.
Mangrove forests in Guinea are classified as public property under the public maritime domain. This means
they are owned by the State and cannot be privately owned or transferred. The primary challenges for
obtaining ownership of mangroves include:
● Inalienability: the public maritime domain is inalienable, imprescriptible, and unseizable,
meaning the state cannot cede ownership or allow private acquisition through occupation.
● Legal restrictions: existing laws, such as the Environmental Code and Maritime Code,
explicitly state that mangroves are part of the public domain, preventing any form of private
ownership or long-term leases.
According to the Environmental Code, the State of Guinea can conduct conventions with third parties that
can contribute to the protection of the environment. Entities can obtain temporary occupation permits or

Page 18
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
18
concessions from the state, allowing them to manage or exploit mangrove areas without transferring
ownership.
This section will be appropriately updated in the PDD submitted for validation.

the completion of the first step of the FPIC process in the first

end of March 2026.

1.12. Description of the Project Activity
The overall project objective is to generate high-quality carbon credits based on greenhouse gases (GHGs)
emission reduction and removal, that will sustainably finance the project and result in economic benefits

Page 19
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
19
for the local communities. GHGs emission reductions are expected to be generated by avoiding unplanned
deforestation by providing alternative income to local communities through the implementation of a series
of activities, including ecotourism, beekeeping, aquaculture, and education campaigns. Alternatives to the
current cooking methods and salt production systems will be also introduced to reduce pressure on
mangrove forests.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) removals will be generated by restoring areas of degraded mangrove forests and
recovering mangrove vegetation cover with the involvement of local communities, supporting local
livelihoods and alleviating poverty.
The project will protect a total of 73,751 hectares from deforestation, contributing to the protection of
coastal communities from climate change, the conservation of floral and faunal diversity and climate
change mitigation.
The project’s climate benefits over the crediting period include the net avoided emissions of 3,374,658
tCO2e.
Blue Coast Carbon will deploy large scale reforestation with community participation through the following
strategic blue carbon conservation activities:
1. Mangrove conservation awareness and education, and training of communities in sustainable
forest management;
2. Mangrove restoration and sustainable mangrove forest management with community-led
monitoring and surveillance;
3. Promoting the adoption of fuel-efficient small wood cookstoves and sustainable solutions for fish
smoking and salt production;
4. Promoting the adoption of sustainable alternative livelihoods, such as ecotourism, beekeeping and
aquaculture, for income diversification.
Blue Coast Carbon will conduct research, engage with community partners, and pilot different project
activities during the early stages of project implementation (i.e., in 2026). The most successful project
activities will be piloted through continuous community consultation. Community engagement will be
carried out following the guidelines established by FPIC. A community consultation plan and protocols to
ensure FPIC of indigenous peoples and local communities (IPLCs) living in and around the project area will
be developed with the collaboration of local partners.
The identified income diversification activities will be piloted in collaboration with experts following thorough
research to determine best practices and learn from the experiences of other projects around the world.
Blue Coast Carbon has been actively working on the feasibility study in Guinea since September 2024. The
project proponent has been active on the ground in Guinea since March 2025. Project activities in Guinea
started with stakeholder mapping, partner selection and the appointment of representatives in Conakry,
Guinea.
The project activities undertaken so far include:

● the full assessment of the Guinea coastline using Blue Coast Carbon’s proprietary data pipeline

● assessment of the carbon sequestration potential of the restoration of degraded mangrove forest

Activity plan
The proposed project activities include the following components:
1. Site preparation:
This step involves carrying out all survey and data collection activities necessary to complete the baseline
assessment. In particular:
- ground survey and mapping of mangrove extension and degradation areas
- in-situ validation of remotely-sensed data
- forest inventory, e.g. map distribution of species in the project area, identification of endangered
species and baseline biodiversity assessment, mangrove propagules supply assessment
- identification of activities needed for ecosystem restoration, e.g. hydrological intervention, pollution
removal. Planting will be carried out only if needed, as the priority will be given to habitat restoration,
because this is known to have higher success rates and faster recovery times.
Seven species of mangrove are found in Guinea: Acrostichum aureum, Avicennia germinans, Conocarpus
erectus, Laguncularia racemosa, Rhizophora harrisonii, Rhizophora mangle, and Rhizophora racemosa.
The species distribution of woody mangroves varies by location. Avicennia spp. needs greater substrate
stability, and is generally found in the shallows along the channels going inland, whereas Rhizophora spp
and Laguncularia prefer convex banks prone to high sedimentation. In-situ surveys will help mapping the
species distribution and selecting the most suitable for planting, if and where needed.
2. Capacity building:
The activities included in this component aim at building capacity amongst local communities and
stakeholders, by training and empowering people in the participation and management of several project
aspects. These include:
- training programmes for local communities on community-based Natural Resource Management
system
- improving the capacity of project staff and government partners on Project Cycle Management

Page 21
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
21
- extending awareness programmes amongst local communities on biodiversity and mangrove
ecosystems
- coordinating implementation of livelihoods/ sustainable community projects with special focus on
women
3. Mangrove restoration and conservation
- Establishment of local management and monitoring committees
- Regular monitoring of field activities, biodiversity, plant re-growth and surveillance
- Set up permanent sample plots for the carbon monitoring
- Identification of leakage areas
4. Community development
- Baseline survey of local communities on their livelihood systems based on Sustainable Development
Goals (SDGs). Conducting socio-economic surveys with regular monitoring in the proposed area, to
collect data on number of people in households, occupation, living condition, education level, income,
fuel-wood consumption, commercial fish harvesting, etc. These data will serve the purpose of setting a
baseline to monitor project impacts on livelihood standard of the community
- Formulating potential sustainable energy, fishery and agriculture practices for local community,
including also sustainable cookstove and salt production
- Developing income generation activities to secure local livelihood improvements
5. Project management, monitoring and evaluation
- Day-to-day technical and financial project management
- Project plan implementation monitoring and adjustment
- Monitoring, verification and reporting
There is not currently any compliance market, such as an Emissions Trading System (ETS) or cap-and-trade
system, nor any Article 6 Framework in force or under development in Guinea5.
The project will not operate in an area covered under a Jurisdictional REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from
Deforestation and Forest Degradation in Developing Countries), as the Guinean government has not
submitted any programme (REDD+ Web Platform accessed on the 3rd February 2026).
Guinea is a signatory to the Paris Agreement, and has presented its revised Nationally Determined
Contribution in 2025 (3rd revision), which covers the forestry sector. Guinea has expressed its willingness
to engage in the voluntary carbon market, but it has not provided specific information about how it plans
to do so. Nonetheless, the Government of Guinea has committed to create a Carbon Market Office (Cellule
5 International Carbon Action, 2025 https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets

Nationale Carbone) which oversees projects, deals with Corresponding Adjustments and other
requirements related to the Carbon Market (e.g. BTRs).
1.13. Project Location
The proposed project site is located along the northern coasts of Guinea, adjacent to the border with
Guinea-Bissau. The project site lies within the administrative regions of Boké.
Blue Coast Carbon has identified two suitable areas for the implementation of a mangrove conservation
project (Figure 1), which were selected based on the forest maturity and the level of deforestation threat.
Figure 1 Areas proposed for Blue Coast Carbon project implementation
Site 1 – North-Frontier and Site 2 – Centre-North are located in the north of the Country, next to the border
with Guinea-Bissau, and south from Kamsar, respectively (Figure 2). These sites include the Marine
Protected Areas of Iles Tristao and Rio Kapatchez, designated Ramsar Wetlands of International
importance (see Section 1.1). Site 1 has a total of 62,683 ha of mangrove forests, while mangroves cover
a total of 11,068 ha in Site 2.
In total, the proposed project sites include 73,751 ha of mangrove forests.

1.14. Conditions Prior to Project Initiation
Avoided mangrove deforestation:
Ecosystem type: Mangrove forests encompassing pristine mangrove areas and degraded/deforested
mangrove areas along Guinea’s coast over a coastal mud substrate.
Current and historical land use: The current and historical land use is mangrove forests with areas that
have been degrading rapidly due to unsustainable overharvesting of mangrove wood.
Mangrove restoration:
Ecosystem type: Degraded/deforested mangrove forests, abandoned mangrove rice fields and areas used
for solar salt no longer operated
Current and historical land use: The area used to be covered by mangrove forests that have been
deforested for fuelwood and charcoal, especially for fish-smoking and salt production, and for mangrove
rice cultivation. These are currently abandoned degraded areas.
Analysis of satellite imagery shows that targeted restoration areas have been cleared of mangroves more
than 10 years from the project start date.
Environmental conditions of the project area
Topography: The coast of Guinea is approximately 300 km long and is featured by sand and mud, estuaries
rich in mangroves, and a wide continental shelf favouring the amplification of the tides. The coast is

Page 24
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
24
indented, with rias (drowned river valleys) that form inlets, tidal marshes, mangrove forests, and estuaries.
The continental shelf of Guinea extends 300 km along the coast, and covers an area of 47,400 km2, making
it the largest continental shelf in West Africa6.
Climate: The West African coast has a subtropical to tropical climate, primarily influenced by the Atlantic
Ocean and the Sahara Desert7. The West African monsoon, a seasonal low-level atmospheric circulation
pattern, represents, along with the Harmattan system, the primary driver of climate variability in the region.
The coasts of Guinea are located within the Guineo-Congolian bioclimatic region, which is the wettest in
West Africa, with average annual rainfall between 2,200 and 5,000 mm. The rainfall can be distributed
across most of the year, or in two rainy seasons with short drier periods between the rains.
Figure 3 Mean annual rainfall 1981–2014, with the number of months of 50 mm or more of rainfall (Adapted
from CILSS, 2016).
Hydrology & hydrodynamics: The most important rivers originate in the Guinea highlands and include the
Niger, Volta, and Senegal rivers 89. For hydroelectric power generation, irrigation, and flood control
purposes, most of these large rivers as well as smaller ones have been dammed in recent decades,
6 UNEP. 2007. “Mangroves of Western and Central Africa.” UNEP-Regional Seas Programme/UNEP-WCMC.
7 Lewis K, Buontempo C (2016) Climate impacts in the Sahel and West Africa: the role of climate science in
policy making”, https://doi.org/10.1787/5jlsmktwjcd0-enresilient coasts (worldbank.org)
8 Diop S, Fabres J, Pravettoni R, Barusseau JP, Descamps C, Ducrotoy JP (2014) The western and central africa
land–sea interface: a vulnerable, threatened, and important coastal zone within a changing environment. In: The
land/ocean interactions in the coastal zone of west and Central Africa (pp. 1–8). Springer, Cham
9 Anthony EJ (2015) Patterns of sand spit development and their management implications on deltaic, drift

(eds) Sand and gravel spits coastal research library series 12. Springer, Berlin, pp 21–36

Page 25
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
25
significantly altering their hydrology and sediment flows, accelerating coastal erosion downstream8910. The
West African coast is generally considered a storm-free environment, dominated by North Atlantic distant
swells1112 with their interannual fluctuation described by the North Atlantic Oscillation8. The wave regime
in the Gulf of Guinea area is mainly driven by extratropical storms, and their variability is modulated by the
South Atlantic Annular Mode (SAM)1314. The evolution of the sandy coast is controlled by strong longshore
sediment drift resulting from oblique waves1115. Tidal amplitude is typically micro- to meso-tidal, with the
highest amplitudes recorded in Guinea, Guinea-Bissau and Sierra Leone (2.8–4.7 m)8.
Biodiversity, ecosystems & vegetation: The richness of estuaries, deltas, coastal lagoons, and nutrient-rich
cold water upwelling contributes greatly to the biodiversity in West Africa. These habitats include (1)
wetlands, particularly those surrounding mangroves in a succession of deltas and estuaries, providing key
habitats for migratory birds16; (2) coastal freshwater lagoons, deltas and estuaries, and a wide range of
tidal marshes and seasonal swamps, also counting with seagrass beds located off some estuaries,
archipelagos and deltas; (3) sandy beaches, considered important nesting ecosystems, especially for sea
turtles. The dominant factor affecting the waters of the continental shelf is coastal upwelling, which is the
source of the rich fish production of the region.
Guinea’s coastal and marine areas are characterised by the presence of still-preserved ecosystems,
including large mangrove zones and rich natural-resource waters that are habitats for important plant and
animal species, including the endangered West African manatee, pygmy hippos, a variety of Cetacea, and
critically endangered migratory birds.
In western Guinea, two ecoregions characterize some 300 km of Atlantic coastline and coastal plains — the
Plaines Côtières (PC – Coastal Plains) and Zones de mangroves (ZM – Mangrove Zones).

Mangroves are found all along the Guinean coast except for Cape Verga and Kaloum Island. The topography
of the coastal area facilitates the deposition of sediment and submersion of the mouths of the rivers. There
is a long tidal reach up the estuaries, which causes flooding of the rivers, leaving raised bars. It is here that
mangroves can develop, within the bay of the estuary. Mangroves extend more than 10 km inland and,
along the widest rivers, they can be found up to 40 km inland from the coast17.
The maximum possible area suitable for mangroves in Guinea, based on geomorphology, is estimated to
be around 4,000 km2 18. Of these, approximately 1,300 m2 of land currently do not have any mangrove
cover because these areas have been cleared for agriculture, salt production, or for increased urbanization,
including the building of ports. Others are simply lying abandoned. The remaining 2,700 km2 currently
under mangrove cover also faces various levels of degradation.
17 Profile, C. 2005. “Global Forest Resources Assessment 2005: Thematic Study on Mangroves.”
18 Based on the conversion of an estimated 1,400 km2 of mangrove swamp being converted to rice fields,
of which 620 km2 lay abandoned in 1993. (Spaulding 1997)

Page 27
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
27
Common mangrove species found in Guinea: Seven species of mangrove are found in Guinea: Acrostichum
aureum, Avicennia germinans, Conocarpus erectus, Laguncularia racemosa, Rhizophora harrisonii,
Rhizophora mangle, and Rhizophora racemosa. The species distribution of woody mangroves varies by
location. Avicennia needs greater substrate stability, and is generally found in the shallows along the
channels going inland, whereas Rhizophora and Laguncularia prefer convex banks prone to high
sedimentation.
All Guinean species are listed as ‘least concern’ on the IUCN Red List of threatened species19.
The non-woody mangroves of Guinea tend to be located in degraded areas20. In denuded areas, Avicennia
and Rhizophora are found in mixed settlements along the banks of the channels. More developed “forest
cathedrals” are found along the Konkouré River where there is fresh water from inland. Avicennia
germinans and grassy species often colonize the deforested areas intended for rice growing. Rhizophora
racemosa can reach 25 m in height in Kakounsou and in the Bay of Sangaréya, but in other areas the trees
seldom exceed 8 m and are often much smaller. In the same zone, Avicennia germinans grows up to 15
m, and Conocarpus erectus can also be found here21.

One of the specificities of the mangrove areas of Guinea is the existence of three specific types of plains:
● Estuarine plains. These border the estuaries of the mouths of coastal rivers. They are very
submersible, and are naturally occupied by Rhizophora mudflats (which are dominant).
● The seafront plains. These are located in sectors further from the mouths of rivers. They are much
less submersible than the estuarine plains, but with salty soils. They were originally occupied by
Avicennia; since the 1950s they have been used for rice cultivation.
● The back mangrove plains. These are floodable (especially during the rainy seasons). They are
found in the transition between continental (non‑salty) brackish and salty environments, and are
partially colonized by hydrophytes with drainage constraints.
Mangroves in Guinea provide habitats and feeding grounds for several migratory shorebird species,
offshore fisheries, and important marine species. The common bird species include the African spoonbill
(Platalea alba), common pratincole (Glareola nuchaltis), the near threatened curlew (Numenius arquata)
and the vulnerable Rufus fishing owl (Scotopelia ussheri)2223.
Vertebrate faunae include the threatened West African manatee (Trichechus senegalensis), the Water
Chevrotain (Hyemoschus aquaticus) and the common Bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus). The
Konkouré and Tristao Ramsar sites are home to the vulnerable African dwarf crocodile (Osteolaemus
tetraspis), the Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus), and the African sharp-nosed crocodile (Mecistops
cataphractus). Other reptile species include the common Senegal mabuya (Trachylepis affinis), the rare
Nimba snake-eyed skink (Panaspis tristaoi), the half-toed gecko (Hemidactylus albivertebralis) and the
African rock python (Python sebae).
Primates including the endangered Red Colobus monkey (Procolobus badius), the small green monkey
(Cercopithecus sabeus) and the common patas monkey (Erytrocebus patas) can also be spotted in the
mangroves of Guinea. Guinea’s beaches are breeding grounds for leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea),
loggerhead (Caretta caretta), green (Chelonia mydas), and olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea) sea turtles
22 Thiollay, JM. Important Bird Areas in Africa and Associated Islands. Priority Sites for Conservation.
2001. Biodiversity and Conservation 11, 1697–1698 (2002). https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016864606424
23 Guinea - BirdLife Country Profile, accessed on the 29th September 2025
https://datazone.birdlife.org/country/factsheet/guinea

and the mangroves provide important nursery areas for juvenile sea turtles and fish. Fish species of
commercial importance found in Guinea’s mangroves include the Tilapia spp, the endangered Senegalese
otolith (Pseudotolithus senegalensis), the near threatened Sea banana (Albula vulpes), and mullets (Mugil
cephalus), shrimp (Palaemon hastatus) and crabs (Portunus validus)24.
Land-use pressures on mangrove forests: The country’s coastal areas are subject to a number of
environmental impacts arising from population growth and development within the country’s key economic
sectors (agriculture, fisheries, mining, and infrastructure). Rapid population growth has resulted in
increased exploitation of coastal resources like mangroves and fisheries, many of which raise issues of
sustainability.
The most common use of mangroves in Guinea is as fuelwood and charcoal, especially for fish-smoking
and salt production. Mangrove wood is also used for construction purposes, including the roofing of houses.
Currently the conversion of mangrove wetlands for salt production, and the expansion of towns and villages
are major destructive threats to mangroves in Guinea25.
In West Africa, including Guinea, salt is either produced by cooking (i.e. evaporation using heat generated
by firewood) or by sun-dried crystallization. The cooked salt consumes a considerable amount of wood from
the mangrove while the sun-dried salt is less productive in the local communities. In Guinea, it is estimated
that the production of 1 kg of salt requires 3.1 kg mangrove wood26.
To produce salt, the mangrove vegetation is removed in selected areas and the underlying soils are dug up
to a depth of around 10 cm to facilitate evaporation. After a few days, the upper crusts are raked and
scraped and, finally, collected into heaps for processing. These soils are leached several times with the
same water and the saline solution is then boiled to obtain crystallized salt. The firewood requirement is
met by the neighbouring mangroves. The environmental consequences of such salt production include the
formation of barren depressions in which the hydrological regime is modified, destruction of mangroves for
firewood, compaction of the surface soil by repeated raking and trampling, and the creation of ecological
conditions unsuitable for the recolonization of mangroves.
Current estimates indicate that approximately 220,000 tonnes of mangrove cuttings is in direct use each
year for salt manufacturing, fish curing, and as fuelwood and timber in Conakry and in rural areas of the
country. However, the annual natural mangrove wood growth per year in the 1,000 km2 of commercially
suitable area is only 80,000–150,000 tonnes, depending on the type of mangroves. This clearly
demonstrates a reason for the loss of mangrove cover from overexploitation. However, it also shows that if
24 Beth A. Polidoro et al., “The Status of Marine Biodiversity in the Eastern Central Atlantic (West and Central
Africa),” Aquatic Conservation: Marine and Freshwater Ecosystems 27, no. 5 (October 2017): 1021–34,
https://doi.org/10.1002/aqc.2744
25 International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (2023). West Africa Coastal Areas High-Level Platform
Benefits of Mangrove Afforestation and Restoration Programs in Guinea-Conakry.

Page 31
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
31
all 2,700 km2 can be made commercially suitable, the annual sustainable yield would range from
210,000–410,000 tonnes, and could help to arrest the degradation of mangrove areas.
The clearing of mangroves for fuelwood and charcoal, timber, and salt extraction has resulted in mangrove
degradation, and expansion of the port of Kamsar in the Bay of Sangaréya has resulted in the loss of
700,000 m2 of mangroves. Fortunately, reforestation of the same area using the Rhizophora and Avicennia
species was undertaken between 1993 and 1998 to help mitigate these effects27.
The extractive industry is also increasingly space-consuming in Guinea. The extraction of bauxite, an ore
needed to manufacture aluminium, is on the rise since 201428. In 2020, Guinea was the world's second-
largest producer of bauxite and has the largest reserves in the world (25%)29. Most of the production (80%)
is located in the Boké region in the north of the Country. The processing and transport of bauxite that takes
place in the coastal zone has also affected the coastal ecosystem, although the extent of the impact has
not been studied extensively.
Losses of mangrove areas have also been caused by the reclamation of land for agriculture. Mangrove rice
cultivation is widespread in Guinea. It is made possible by mangrove bunds that protect the land from
flooding. Most of the land used for rice cultivation has been obtained over time by clearing erstwhile
mangrove plantations.
Twenty-three percent of the national rice production in Guinea is from mangrove areas, and it provides
livelihoods for more than 50,000 rice farmers, the majority of whom are women. Shifting to agriculture also
occurs where salt inundation is low. Mangrove rice is a flood-fed crop requiring two flooding cycles, one
with freshwater and one with saltwater. The saltwater is needed to eliminate weeds, regulate soil pH, and
deposit organic matter and nutrients. Freshwater is necessary for soil desalination prior to cultivation, and
maintenance of the water table throughout the cycle.
In ideal conditions, mangrove rice farming produces higher yields than other rice farming techniques used
in the interior of the country. Annual mangrove rice production averages around 376,000 tonnes; it
represents 16% of rice farmland in the country, and 23% of national production30.
Of an estimated 1,400 km2 of mangrove that had been converted to rice fields in Guinea by 1993, 620
km2 had been abandoned31. The accelerated rate of conversion of mangrove forests to rice in Guinea has
resulted in irreversible damage to these forests.
Sea level rise & erosion: In addition to mangroves being cut to support subsistence rural livelihoods and
conversion to rice fields, sea-level rise and other climatic phenomena are also contributing toward
27 UNEP. 2007. “Mangroves of Western and Central Africa.” UNEP-Regional Seas Programme/UNEP-WCMC.
28 Initiative pour la transparence dans les industries extractives en Guinée. Rapport Assoupli 2019-2020.
https://www.itie-guinee.org/rapport-assoupli-exercices-2019-2020/"
29 https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2021/mcs2021-bauxite-alumina.pdf
30 Agence Franç aise de Developpement 2016
31 Spalding M. , F. Biasco, C Field 1997. Word Mangrove Atlas. International Society or Mangrove Ecosystems.
Okinawa, Japan.

Page 32
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
32
mangrove degradation in Guinea. These occur through the loss of coastal and intertidal habitats, including
changes in geomorphological processes, and the increased vulnerability of woody formations (UNDP 2019).
Studies also reveal that sea-level rise is a major potential threat to mangrove ecosystems due to their
sensitivity to the duration and frequency of flooding, and salinity levels that may exceed the physiological
threshold of mangrove-specific tolerance. Additionally, the failure to maintain dikes built in previous
decades, and the lack of planning and integration of climate risks in construction activities on the coast
have contributed to the coastal zone’s vulnerability to erosion, and have affected the mangroves. Sea-level
rise will increase the direct inundation of low-lying areas, facilitate rapid erosion of the soft shores, and
increase offshore loss of sediment as well as flooding.
The projected total sea level is expected to raise by 0.78 m by 2100, based on the sea level projections
relative to the period 1995-2014 for the West African region for Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)
scenario SSP5-8.5 (very high GHG emissions), as defined by the 6th Assessment Report from the IPCC32.
Figure 5 Sea level projections relative to the period 1995-2014 for the West African region32.
It is estimated that a 1 m increase in sea level will inundate a significant portion of the coastal areas,
causing major problems for mangrove rice cultivation.
Mangrove deforestation trends: Estimates show that Guinea currently has a little over 2,000 km2 of
mangrove forests, down from 4,000 in 19573334. Between 1980 and 2006, it is estimated that the
mangrove area in Guinea fell from 2,992 to 2,039 km2, representing a loss of 32 %2735. A 2019 survey by
NASA estimated the mangrove area to be 2,076 km2.
32 Data accessed through the NASA Sea Level Projection Tool
33 Diallo M. et al. 2019: Model of Criteria Taking into Account Halieutic Biodiversity in Strategic Port Planning in
Guinea.” Vertigo: The electronic journal in environmental sciences, vol.19 n° 3.
34 Rouanet 1957, cited in Kaba, B. 2001
35 Ajonina, G., A. Diamé, and J. Kairo. 2008. “Current Status and Conservation of Mangroves in Africa: An
Overview.” World Rainforest Movement Bulletin 133: 1–6.

VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
33
According to the Global Mangrove Watch, in 2020 the area of mangrove habitat in Guinea was 2,211.45
km2, with a deforestation rate between 2010 and 2020 of 1.9% 36. Estimates reveal that only about 1,000
km2 of this total area is in a good enough state that it could allow for commercial exploitation of mangroves
if done on a sustainable basis37.
Socio-economic situation: Despite its abundant natural resources, growing population, and privileged
geographic location, 52% of Guineans live below the international poverty line of $3.65 a-day, with the
poverty rate increasing by 7% between 2019 and 202438. This limited poverty reduction is due to weak
productivity growth resulting from low levels of physical and human capital, declining competitiveness of
non-mining sectors, and significant structural inequalities in income, education, and infrastructure.
Figure 6 Contribution to inflation in Guinea (left) and poverty rates and real GDP per capita (right)36.
Food inflation is elevated and is the main driver of inflation in Guinea, contributing 3.3% to the national
annual inflation rate of 5.1% in 2024. The increase in food prices disproportionately affects the poor, with
low-income populations being particularly vulnerable as they spend a larger share of their income on food.
Persistent food inflation could exacerbate food insecurity in Guinea where the prevalence of severe food
insecurity among the total population is already high, estimated at 50%. In fact, despite real GDP per capita
increasing by 3.1% in 2024, the poverty rate (<$3.65-a-day in 2017) increased by 0.3ppts to 52% due to
slightly higher annual inflation and insufficient non-mining sector job creation38.
36 www.globalmangrovewatch.org (accessed on 6th November 2025)
37 RUË O. (1998): The development of the coast of Guinea - Memories of mangroves - ed. The Harmattan
38 World Bank. 2025. Guinea Economic Update: Domestic Resource Mobilization and Management for Inclusive
and Sustainable Development, DC: World Bank.

Page 34
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
34
Female-headed households are more vulnerable to poverty due to lower educational attainment. Women
aged 25-35 are 19% more likely to live in poverty compared to men (43.4% vs. 24.4%). This is exacerbated
by the school enrolment gap for girls, which widens at the secondary level. The lack of investment in
women’s human capital increases their poverty risk and limits their economic participation. Limited
intergenerational mobility in education perpetuates poverty across generations. Nationally, 73% of adults
whose fathers lacked formal education also lack formal education, with the share rising to 84% in rural
areas. This suggests persistent income disparities and inequality unless access to education is expanded38.
Women living in coastal areas are heavily dependent on mangrove products, further highlighting their
vulnerability39.
1.15. Compliance with Laws, Statutes and Other Regulatory Frameworks
The project will be in line with all laws and statutory requirements of Guinea such as the Civil Code (2019)
and the ones regarding :
Labour: Guinea Labor Code (Loi N°L/2014/072/CNT portant Code du travail) especially the articles about
working conditions and presidential decree of 1st June 2022 regarding the new Guinean Minimum Salary;
Land ownership: Land law in Guinea is governed by the following texts:
• Constitution of 2010, which guarantees its citizens the right to private property.
• The Guinea Land Code of 1992 (Code Foncier et Domanial), which stipulates that the owner is the
person who provides proof of the occupation of a plot of land through its use (creation of value) or through
a public inquiry40. This law establishes access to individual property for individuals and legal entities, while
maintaining the presumption of State ownership of vacant and unowned land. This reform also creates land
commissions in each prefecture of Guinea41. This law was essentially designed to address urban
specificities: only Article 92 addresses the issue of rural land tenure, albeit in a very vague manner.
• The Rural Land Policy of 2001 (Déclaration de la Politique Foncière en Milieu Rural) acknowledges
specific customary land rights and encourages the creation of laws to formalize these rights with an
increase of local participation. However, this policy was not accompanied by implementation measures.
39 WACA (2023). Technical Report: Understanding the Nexus of Mangroves and Women in Guinea-Conakry.
https://www.wacaprogram.org/knowledge/technical-report-understanding-nexus-mangroves-and-women-
guinea-conakry
40 Article 39: The following are owners within the meaning of this Code: 1° - natural or legal persons holding a
land title; 2° - occupants, natural or legal persons, holders of a land register, residence permit or occupation
permit; 3° - occupants, natural or legal persons, who can prove that they have occupied a building peacefully,
personally, continuously and in good faith and as owner. If necessary, proof of good faith shall be provided by all
means, in particular by payment of property taxes relating to the said building, by the development of the building
in accordance with local customs or by a public and adversarial inquiry.
41 Diop, Moustapha. 2017. Réformes foncières et gestion des ressources naturelles en Guinée : enjeux de
patrimonialité et de propriété dans le Timbi au Fouta Djalon. Paris: Karthala.
https://landportal.org/library/resources/9782845868564/r%C3%A9formes-fonci%C3%A8res-et-gestion-des-
ressources-naturelles-en-guin%C3%A9e.

Page 35
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
35
The process of revising the land laws, which began in 2012, has still not been completed 10 years after its
launch42.
• The Pastoral Rights Law of 1995 (Loi L/95/51/CTRN portant Code Pastoral) provides herders with
open and unrestricted access to pastoral areas and the natural resources within them, with the condition
of avoiding overuse and respecting the customary rights of other users.
Forests and restoration:
- Guinea’s Forestry Code (Loi ordinaire U2017/060/AN du 12 décembre 2017, portant code forestier de
la République de Guinée) especially articles 51, 67, 124, 128, 137 and 142 which encourage forest
restoration.
- Guinea’s Environmental Code (Decret D/2019/221/PRG/SGG portant promulgation de la loi L/2019/00
34/AN du 04 juillet 2019) especially article 38 and 39.
-Wildlife Protection Code and Hunting Regulations (Loi Ordinaire N° 2018/0049/AN Portant Code de
protection de la faune sauvage et réglementation de la chasse and Arrêté A/2020/1591/MEEF/CAAB/SGG
Portant protection des espèces de faune et de flore sauvages en République de Guinée).
Water:
- Code Maritime regulates the maritime waters under the jurisdiction or sovereignty of the Republic of
Guinea, vessels registered in the Republic of Guinea, their crews, and passengers on board, the crews and
passengers of foreign vessels, and floating platforms located in waters under national jurisdiction.
- Code de la Pêche maritime, regulating maritime fishing in the Republic of Guinea, defines the rules
applicable to fishing in the maritime zones under Guinean sovereignty or jurisdiction, as well as the rules
applicable to Guinean fishing vessels operating beyond these zones.
- Code de l’Eau regulates water resources, including a set of measures to be taken to ensure their
permanent quantitative and qualitative inventory, protection, enhancement, and optimal use, taking into
account the social, economic, and cultural needs of the nation.
In addition, Guinea is a signatory to the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative (AFR100) which is
a pan-African effort aimed at restoring 100 million hectares of deforested and degraded landscapes across
the African continent by 2030. This ambitious initiative seeks to address critical issues such as land
degradation, climate change mitigation, and biodiversity conservation. AFR100 brings together a diverse
range of stakeholders, including governments, local communities, non-governmental organizations, and
42 https://data.landportal.org/book/narratives/2022/guinea#ref7

Page 36
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
36
private sector partners, to collaborate on large-scale restoration projects. Within this framework, Guinea
aims to restore 55% of degraded land and restrict the loss of undegraded land to 1% before 203043.
There is currently no specific legislation for mangrove forests in Guinea. However, the importance of
mangroves for the climate, biodiversity, and society is recognized by state actors, and policy frameworks
are being developed at the national and regional levels for this habitat.
The Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is responsible for:
● developing the Mangrove Management Master Plan;
● consulting with communities in mangrove areas affected by high deforestation rates;
● proposing solutions to mangrove degradation.
However, Guinea has not yet established dedicated coastal protected areas, and mangrove forests are only
partially included in protected areas.
Other weaknesses related to the protection of mangrove forests include a limited capacity of government
institutions to reform, weak academic training, and a lack of resources to monitor and enforce regulations
on the ground.
Furthermore, the laws governing protected areas are sometimes contradictory. For example, the Ministry
of the Environment is legally responsible for the management of classified forests, but in practice, the
prefect is also authorized to grant occupancy permits to individuals, without taking mangroves into account
in the absence of a clear legal framework.
Protected areas are poorly defined; they include classified forests, national parks, etc., but this definition
is not unanimous, and a protected areas code is currently being finalized.
The proposed activities fall within a regulatory framework that is evolving favorably, but conservation
frameworks still lack rigorous enforcement in coastal areas, demonstrating the regulatory overhang of the
project's activities.
43 https://afr100.org/country/guinea#section-projects

1.18. Sustainable Development Contributions
The proposed project will contribute to the achievement of the following five sustainable development goals
(SDGs) of the United Nations’ Agenda 2030:
SDG 5: Gender equality (medium priority)
Monitoring, restoration, and surveillance activities will be carried out directly employing local communities
for the whole duration of the project. Men and women will be involved in equal measure in all project
activities, including stakeholder consultations, ensuring women’s full and effective participation and equal
opportunities at all levels.
This will be monitored by assessing the proportion of work positions held by women in project
implementation and stakeholders consultation, including managerial positions.
The project will oversee the development of side economic activities owned by women, e.g. beekeeping,
aquaculture projects, ecotourism.
SDG 8: Decent work and economic growth (medium priority)
The project will provide direct employment as well as development and entrepreneurship opportunities for
local communities, including through training and professional development, to ensure long-term impact.
The project is also designed to provide alternative livelihoods for the local community by testing and
generating income streams from the project area through carbon, agroforestry, and other economic
activities. Community initiatives will increase incomes and promote sustainable agricultural and fishing
practices to improve living conditions. The protection, restoration and reduction of pollution in mangroves
will also help to enhance food security by protecting fish nurseries and improving them for future fish stocks.
SDG 13: Climate action
The project will restore degraded mangrove forests, aiming at contributing to climate change mitigation by
removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere through mangrove forest restoration and planting. The
new mangrove growth will enhance carbon stocks in biomass and soil. Restoring degraded ecosystems will
capture more than 1,900,000 tonnes of CO2e.
Mangroves provide long-term coastal protection from extreme weather and climate-related events, as they
mitigate erosion and stabilize soil. Their intricate and expansive crown-root systems entrap sediments and
dissipate turbulent kinetic energy which also enhances sediment deposition. Mangroves are also crucial in
mitigating the impact of tropical cyclones and storm surges, and offer substantial protection against wind

Page 39
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
39
damage during storms. Restoring mangroves will thus strengthen coastal resilience to sea level rise and
more intense storms.
SDG 14 Life below water (low priority)
This project aims at establishing a new coastal protected area managed by an ecosystem-based approach,
thus contributing to the achievement of SDG 14. The project area covers threatened coastal habitat that is
under pressure from encroachment, development and pollution.
Furthermore, the high productivity and physical complexity of mangrove ecosystems make them important
nursery grounds for many commercial and non-commercial fish and invertebrate species. The restoration
and conservation activities foreseen will thus contribute to the restoration of fish stocks in Guinea. The
project's restoration activities will promote the recovery of the natural ecosystem, species richness, and
contribute to the reduction of nutrient pollution, thanks to the natural capability of mangroves to filter
organic pollution.
SDG 15: Life on land (deforestation) (low priority)
This project will promote the implementation of sustainable management of mangrove forests, halt
deforestation, restore degraded forests and increase reforestation in Guinea.

Page 40

Stakeholder
Identification
Stakeholders identification will take place following FAO’s FPIC
principles and CCB guidelines.
Blue Coast Carbon will carry out a thorough stakeholder mapping and
analysis before the project starts, to identify who has rights and
interests over the project area, and how every stakeholder relates to
each other and to the project.
We will seek to map both primary and secondary stakeholders.
Primary stakeholders include individuals or groups with statutory or
customary rights to land or resources within the project area, e.g.
Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities, residents in the area,
smallholder farmers, and businesses operating in the project area.
Secondary stakeholders are local, regional, and national authorities
or organizations involved in the region's conservation, restoration, or
development initiatives, e.g., Government agencies and traditional or
customary power structures, Non-Governmental Organizations
(NGOs), Academic or research institutions, non-local businesses
operating around the site or in relevant industries, other local carbon
project proponents or developers.
Once all the relevant stakeholders are identified, Blue Coast Carbon
together with the local partner will analyse living standards, health,
access to infrastructures and facilities, climate change adaptation of
each group. Each stakeholder will be prioritised and selected based
on their importance and influence over the project, to categorise
those to be involved, consulted or informed during each project
phase. The potential impact of the project on the different groups will
also be assessed.
The stakeholders analysis will also include a gender analysis,
assessing the relative positions of women and men in terms of
representation and influence, and the benefits and disincentives
associated with the allocation of tasks to women and men.
Blue Coast Carbon has been working on the ground in Guinea since
March 2025. Since then, the Company has carried out a preliminary
stakeholder mapping, meeting Government representatives and
potential partners. These include the following:
● National government: Ministry of Environment and
Sustainable Development (MEDD), Ministry of Agriculture
and Livestock, National Parks Directorate (OGPNRF)

Section to be completed and updated in the PD submitted for
validation.
Legal or customary
tenure/access rights
Under Articles 53 and 54 of the Maritime Code (2019), all Guinean
mangroves fall within the Maritime Public Domain (DPM). This domain
is inalienable and includes a 100-meter coastal strip and all areas up
to the limit of water salinity. Consequently, while Article 17 of the
Forestry Code allows landowners to own forest products, the
inalienability of the DPM ensures that mangrove land and its
biological resources remain the exclusive property of the State.
Despite State ownership, Articles 46–50 of the Forestry Code
recognize "usage rights" for local communities. These rights permit
subsistence activities, including artisanal fishing, salt production, and
domestic wood collection.
To bridge the gap between statutory State ownership and customary
use, the project will secure tenure through:
Temporary occupation permits, legalising project activities within the
DPM.
Community management agreements, formalising traditional usage
rights into sustainable management contracts under Forestry
Administration oversight.

and changes over time

2.1.2. Stakeholder Consultation and Ongoing Communication
Stakeholder consultation has begun at the national level, with multiple meetings throughout 2025 and into
2026 with the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD). Blue Coast Carbon has also
consulted with numerous other stakeholders and potential partners including National Parks Directorate
(OGPNRF), Biotope, United Nation Development Programme, Charente-Maritime Coopération.
A local stakeholder consultation will be carried out before the implementation of project activities, to make
sure all the stakeholders identified will be involved.
The consultations will be conducted in a manner that is inclusive and respectful of local knowledge.
The full participation of stakeholders in both project design and implementation is key to the project’s
success. Therefore, the local community will be involved in all project stages, from planning to design and
implementation. A stakeholder engagement plan customised to all groups identified, will be co-defined with
key stakeholders. It will include at least the following steps:
● introduction of project to all primary stakeholders, discussing project goals and objectives, outlining
expected outcomes and the project timeline, and introducing the project team
● gathering feedback from all stakeholders through consultations customised to each target group.
At least 2 focus groups will be held separately with only women.
● collection of information necessary for the project development, e.g. traditional uses of mangroves,
sacred sites, history of degradation, historical presence of wildlife on the project site, etc.
● obtaining agreement on project design and activities, by means of co-designing activities.
A grievance management procedure will also be designed to deal with any grievance during the
engagement process and project implementation.
The project proponent will develop a procedure for monitoring and evaluation of decision-making and
engagement processes to allow periodic reviews of the agreement with the community and the engagement
process.
All stakeholders engagement activities will be regularly reported throughout the project duration.

2.1.4. Grievance Redress Procedure
A grievance mechanism will be established to address concerns related to the project in the project area.
This mechanism will align with international best practices and will include steps to identify potential risks,
concerns, and conflicts associated with the project. The system will be designed to enable Indigenous
Peoples and local communities to express their concerns and grievances effectively. An appropriate
grievance mechanism will be drafted to respond to grievances and integrate feedback during the project's
design and implementation phases. A grievance register will be maintained to document all complaints and
how they have been addressed and solved. The information collected will be used to introduce changes in
the project to reduce dispute-related risks and to learn for future projects, and to improve FPIC processes
as the project progresses.

2.2. Risks to Stakeholders and the Environment
2.2.1. Management Experience
Blue Coast Carbon was founded to develop the most reliable nature-based projects for high-integrity carbon
credits. The company’s mission is exploiting carbon markets to support the sustainable development of
low-income Countries. The company specialises in blue carbon projects to contribute to the protection of
marine environments while mitigating climate change and support community development.
The management team has extensive expertise in geospatial data analysis and remote sensing, marine
ecology and cooperative development projects. The team all have over 15 years of experience delivering
advanced remote sensing projects using satellite and drone data across more than 40 countries. We
leverage proprietary data-driven analysis, coastal ecosystem expertise, and industry-standard verification
to originate high-integrity blue carbon credits backed by real-world impact and future resilience. The skill
set within Blue Coast Carbon covers finance, project management, environmental science, carbon offset
projects, community development, technology, and many other areas, including on-ground experience
managing projects and operations in Guinea.
Additional local partners are being identified to support community engagement, rural development, and
project activity implementation.

VM0007 Land in the project area has qualified
as forest for at least the 10 years prior
to the project start date. Mangrove
forests are excluded from any tree
height requirement in a forest
definition, as they consist of 95 %
mangrove species, which often do not
reach the same height as other tree
species. Mangroves occupy contiguous
areas and their functioning as a forest
is independent of tree height.
The forests in the project area
are mangrove forests and are
thus excluded from any tree
height requirements.

modules are applied alongside other
relevant modules

been applied.

3.5. Additionality
Tidal wetland restoration and conservation projects shall apply module VMD0052 ‘Demonstration of
additionality of tidal wetland restoration and conservation project activities’. According to the module, a
project is additional if it meets the requirements for regulatory surplus, and the applicability conditions
(positive list).
3.5.1. Regulatory Surplus
Is the project located in an UNFCCC Annex 1 or Non-Annex 1 country?
☐ Annex 1 country ☒ Non-Annex 1 country
Are the project activities mandated by any law, statute, or other regulatory framework?
☐ Yes ☒ No
If the project is located inside a Non-Annex 1 country and the project activities are mandated by a law,
statute, or other regulatory framework, are such laws, statutes, or regulatory frameworks systematically
enforced?
☐ Yes ☒ No
There are no specific legislations for mangrove forests in Guinea. Nonetheless, mangrove’s importance for
climate, biodiversity and society is recognized by state actors and policy frameworks are being designed
both at national and regional levels for this habitat.
The Ministry of Environment, Water and Forestry is in charge of:
● The Master Plan for the Development of Mangroves;
● consultations with communities in mangrove areas affected by a high rate of deforestation;
● Proposing solutions for mangrove degradation.
However, Guinea has not established dedicated coastal protected areas yet, and mangrove forests are only
partially included in the existing protected areas. This is mostly due to the following:
● Lack of capacity of governmental institutions, limited training, lack of enforcement, lack of
resources.
● Laws governing protected areas are often ambiguous. For example, the Ministry of Environment is
legally responsible for managing classified forests, yet in practice the préfet is also allowed to grant
extraction rights to individuals, although not for mangrove extraction.
● Protected areas are poorly defined; they include classified forests, national parks, etc. but not
everyone agrees with this definition.

Page 64
VCS Project Description Template, v4.4
64
The proposed project activities are not specifically mandated by any regulatory framework and the more
generalist conservation frameworks are not currently being enforced in the coastal areas, which
demonstrates the regulatory surplus of the project activities.
3.5.2. Additionality Methods
The additionality procedure as per module VMD0052 consists of two steps. Step 1 consists in
demonstrating regulatory surplus (see Section 3.5.1), and Step 2 requires the project to meet the
applicability conditions of the module.
The proposed project is compliant with such conditions as project activities restoring tidal wetlands include
the following:
- restoring hydrological conditions (e.g., removing tidal barriers, improving hydrological connectivity,
restoring tidal flow to wetlands) to assist natural recovery of vegetation;
- re-introducing native mangrove communities by means of replanting, where natural recovery is not
possible;
- improving management practices by means of removing invasive species.
Furthermore, project activities conserving tidal wetlands include protecting at-risk mangrove forests from
degradation and deforestation by means of conservation programmes, community awareness campaigns,
and promotion of alternative livelihoods and sustainable wood uses to reduce pressure on mangroves.
Therefore, the proposed project can be considered additional.
